t.alcantarilla bridge@38.9,-6.4:
Mérida was founded by the Romans in 25 BC as Augusta Emerita, a city for veterans of the Cantabrian wars, and it grew into the capital of the province of Lusitania. Few places in Spain carry their Roman past so openly. The small Alcantarilla bridge on the edge of town is one piece of the Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida, listed by UNESCO in 1993, and its name, from the Arabic for little bridge, tells you how many hands this landscape has passed through. It is a quiet, unassuming structure, and that is a good reason to start here before you tackle the big sights.

Those big sights are spectacular. The theatre, with its two-storey stage front of columns, still hosts a classical drama festival in summer. The amphitheatre sits beside it. The long Roman bridge over the Guadiana, with dozens of arches, carried traffic until well into modern times. The tall arches of the aqueduct of Los Milagros, with storks nesting on top, carried water from the Proserpina reservoir north of the city, itself a Roman dam that is still a popular place for a swim on hot days. The National Museum of Roman Art, designed by Rafael Moneo, is one of the best museums in the country.

The riding around Mérida is that of the Extremaduran plains: long straight roads through dehesa, the open woodland of holm and cork oak where black Iberian pigs root for acorns in autumn. It is wide open, hot and sometimes windy, with big skies and very little traffic once you leave the city. South of town, the road to Alange and its reservoir has more curves and hills, and Alange's thermal baths go back to Roman times too. Summer temperatures often climb above forty degrees, so start early and take a long lunch.

Mérida is the regional capital, with fifty-six thousand people, so fuel, food and accommodation are plentiful. Try migas, the shepherd's breadcrumb dish, jamón ibérico from the dehesas around you, and Torta del Casar, a soft sheep's cheese you eat with a spoon. In the evenings the city comes alive late, with tapas bars around the Plaza de España; nobody here dines before nine.
t.monastery of alcobaca@39.6,-9.0:
In 1153, Afonso Henriques, the first king of Portugal, gave a vast estate to the Cistercian monks of Bernard of Clairvaux, and they built here one of the greatest monasteries of medieval Europe. The church of Alcobaça, with its long, soaring nave of pale stone, is austere and beautiful in the Cistercian manner, and the cloisters, dormitory, chapter house and refectory survive almost intact. The kitchen is enormous, with a huge chimney and a stream diverted through it so the monks could catch fish directly. UNESCO listed the monastery in 1989. But the main reason most visitors come is a love story.

In the transepts lie the tombs of King Pedro I and Inês de Castro, his lover, who was murdered in 1355 on the orders of his father, King Afonso IV. When Pedro became king, he took revenge on her killers and, according to legend, had her body exhumed and crowned queen. Their tombs, carved with extraordinary detail, are placed facing each other, so that on the day of the Last Judgement, when they rise, the first thing each sees will be the other. It is one of the great romantic tales of Portugal, retold in poems, plays and operas.

The area around Alcobaça is rich in history. Nearby, the battlefield of Aljubarrota, where the Portuguese defeated a Castilian army in 1385 and secured independence, has a museum, and the monastery of Batalha, built to celebrate the victory, is a masterpiece of Gothic architecture, also listed by UNESCO. To the west, Nazaré is a fishing town famous for its giant waves, which attract surfers from around the world in winter.

The riding here is relaxed, with country roads through orchards, vineyards and pine forests, and the coast road offers views of the Atlantic. Traffic is moderate, but busy around the towns and on summer weekends. Alcobaça, with nearly sixteen thousand inhabitants, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The region is famous for its convent sweets, made with eggs and sugar, and ginja, a sour cherry liqueur. Try frango na púcara, chicken cooked in a clay pot, or fresh fish grilled in Nazaré.
t.cornalvo dam@39.0,-6.2:
Nearly two thousand years after Roman engineers built it, the dam at Cornalvo still holds water. It lies in the rolling countryside north-east of Mérida, in Extremadura, and it supplied the Roman city of Augusta Emerita, capital of the province of Lusitania. The dam is an earthen embankment faced with stone, with a tower in the reservoir that controlled the outflow, and it is part of the Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The reservoir is surrounded by the Cornalvo Natural Park, a landscape of dehesa, the open woodland of holm oaks and cork oaks typical of Extremadura, where black Iberian pigs root for acorns in autumn and cattle and sheep graze among the trees. The park is home to birds such as storks, eagles and vultures, and in spring the meadows are full of wildflowers. Mérida has another Roman dam, Proserpina, closer to the city, and the aqueducts that carried water to the city, especially the Acueducto de los Milagros, are spectacular.

The riding in this part of Extremadura is relaxed and pleasant. The roads are quiet, with long straights and gentle curves through the dehesa, and traffic is light. The landscape is wide and open, with views over rolling hills dotted with oaks. Summer is very hot, often above forty degrees, so ride early in the morning or late in the afternoon, and carry plenty of water. Spring is the best season, when the fields are green and full of flowers, and autumn is pleasant too.

San Pedro de Mérida and Trujillanos are small villages nearby with basic services, and Mérida, fifteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Mérida's Roman monuments, including the theatre, the amphitheatre and the bridge over the Guadiana, are among the most impressive in Spain. The local food is excellent: Iberian ham from acorn-fed pigs, torta del Casar, a creamy sheep's cheese, and migas, fried breadcrumbs with pork. A walk along the crest of the dam in the late afternoon, with storks overhead and the dehesa fading into haze, is the most peaceful hour you will spend in Extremadura.
t.royal building of mafra palace@38.9,-9.3:
King João V of Portugal had a great deal of Brazilian gold and a vow to keep, and the result is the Royal Building of Mafra, a palace, basilica and monastery so large that it seems to belong to a different scale of town altogether. Construction began in 1717, reportedly in thanks for the birth of an heir, and the project absorbed enormous resources and tens of thousands of workers. The facade stretches for some two hundred and twenty metres, with the basilica in the centre and the royal apartments in the wings, the king's at one end and the queen's at the other, a long walk apart.

Inside, the highlights are the basilica, built in pale marble, with six historic organs designed to be played together, and two carillons in the towers, among the largest in the world. The library is the real treasure: a long baroque hall with a patterned marble floor and tens of thousands of leather-bound books, protected, famously, by a colony of small bats that come out at night and eat the insects that would otherwise damage the volumes. The building was listed by UNESCO in 2019, along with the Tapada Nacional de Mafra, the walled royal hunting park next door, where deer and wild boar still roam among the cork oaks.

Mafra is a town of twelve thousand people in the hills north-west of Lisbon, and it makes a good base for exploring the coast. Ericeira, eight kilometres away, is a fishing town turned surfing capital, with white houses on the cliffs and seafood restaurants overlooking the beach; its coastline is a recognised world surfing reserve. The roads between Mafra, Ericeira and Sintra wind through hills, pine woods and farmland, with good curves and views of the Atlantic, though traffic can be heavy on weekends and in summer.

South of Mafra, the Sintra hills rise up, covered in forest and topped with palaces, a wonderful but busy area. The road up to the Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe, is a classic ride, with a strong wind from the ocean. The Atlantic weather can be changeable, with fog in summer mornings and showers in spring.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy in Mafra. Try pão de Mafra, the local bread, with chouriço, or a plate of grilled fish in Ericeira. And in the basilica square, look up at the facade and try to imagine what it took to build.
t.the roman circus@38.9,-6.3:
Mérida was founded in 25 BC as Augusta Emerita, a city for veterans of the Cantabrian Wars, and it grew into the capital of the Roman province of Lusitania. Few places in Spain carry their Roman past so openly. The circus lies on the eastern side of town, a long, flat oval of grass more than four hundred metres from end to end, with the low remains of the central barrier and the seating banks around it. It once held tens of thousands of spectators for chariot races, and though the stands are mostly gone, you can still walk the track and picture the teams thundering around the turning posts.

The rest of the Roman city is just as impressive. The theatre, with its two-storey stage wall of columns, still hosts a classical drama festival every summer. The amphitheatre stands beside it. The Puente Romano crosses the Guadiana in a long procession of arches, now pedestrian, and the National Museum of Roman Art, designed by Rafael Moneo, is one of the finest museums of its kind anywhere. Out of town, the Romans built two dams to supply water, Proserpina and Cornalvo, both still holding water, and the remaining arches of the aqueduct of Los Milagros stride across the valley of the Albarregas, with storks nesting on top.

The riding in Extremadura is about space. Long roads cross open dehesa, the parkland of holm oaks where black Iberian pigs forage for acorns, and the horizon stays wide in every direction. The old Roman road north, the Vía de la Plata, is followed by the modern A-66 and the N-630, and the smaller roads east towards Alange, a spa village with Roman baths still in use, are quieter and more pleasant. Do not expect mountain curves near Mérida; expect wide skies, lazy bends and a lot of light.

The climate is the main warning. Summer temperatures in Extremadura regularly climb above forty degrees, and riding in July afternoons is punishing. Spring, when the dehesa is green and covered in flowers, is the best season, and autumn is good too.

Mérida has everything a rider needs: fuel, workshops, hotels, and tapas bars serving jamón ibérico from the region, migas, and the torta del Casar, a soft, pungent sheep's cheese from near Cáceres.
t.thermal baths at alange@38.8,-6.2:
The Romans, who were serious about hot water, found a warm spring at Alange in what is now Extremadura and built a bathing complex around it, and the place is still used today. The Roman baths, about twenty kilometres from Mérida, include a domed chamber with stone benches and a pool fed by the spring, and the water comes out pleasantly warm, a gift in a dry country. The baths date from the time when Mérida, then called Emerita Augusta, was one of the great cities of Roman Spain, and wealthy citizens would travel here to relax and be cured.

The setting is a small white town on a hill, below the ruins of a Moorish castle, overlooking a reservoir and a landscape of cork oak and holm oak, olive groves and open pasture. This type of woodland, called dehesa, shelters black Iberian pigs that feed on acorns, and the ham that comes from them is among the finest in the world. Cranes winter in the area, and storks nest on rooftops and church towers across the region. The sky is huge and the light in summer evenings is a warm gold.

Riding in Extremadura is generous and relaxed. Roads are quiet, wide and well surfaced, with long straights across the plain and gentle curves where they cross the hills, and in spring the fields are green and speckled with wildflowers. The summer heat is severe, with temperatures above forty degrees, so ride early or late, and drink plenty of water. Autumn brings mushrooms, acorn harvests and milder weather, and winter is cool but rarely harsh. Livestock can wander onto the road, especially in the dehesa, and storks sometimes land in the middle of nowhere.

Alange has a couple of cafés and bars and the spa itself, and Zarza de Alange nearby has a shop or two. For fuel, check at Guareña, about fifteen kilometres off, or head to Mérida, with its Roman theatre, amphitheatre and the high aqueduct, which is worth a stop on its own. Local food leans toward cured pork, migas and sheep's cheese, and you can finish with a slice of cake made from almonds. Bring swimming gear if you plan to use the baths, and check opening times first.
t.proserpina dam@39.0,-6.4:
The Romans built dams in Spain on a scale that still surprises engineers, and Proserpina, a few kilometres north of Mérida, is one of the best preserved. It was built in the first or second century AD to store water for Emerita Augusta, the provincial capital, which was fed by aqueduct from the lake. The dam is a massive earthen embankment faced with stone and backed by huge buttresses, some four hundred metres long, and it has held water for roughly nineteen centuries with repairs. The reservoir, a long green lake in a landscape of holm oak and rock, is now a place where local people fish, swim and walk.

The name of the dam comes from the goddess Proserpina, whom Roman citizens honoured with a small temple that stood near the shore. Mérida itself, six kilometres away, was founded in 25 BC for veterans of the army and became one of the great cities of the empire in the west, and you can still visit its theatre, amphitheatre, circus, bridge over the Guadiana, and the arches of the Los Milagros aqueduct, which carried water from Proserpina to the city. UNESCO listed the whole as an archaeological ensemble in 1993.

The approach is easy riding. Quiet lanes lead from Mérida through farmland to the reservoir, with gentle bends and dehesa on either side, and the surfaces are generally good. On summer weekends locals come to the water and cars park along the verge, so watch for pedestrians and children. The heat is a serious matter from June to September, and the best times are spring and autumn. Storks and kites circle overhead, and the air smells of dry grass and thyme.

Mérida has everything you need: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and rooms, and nearby Esparragalejo and Mirandilla have smaller services. Look for cured ham, a rich stew of pork and chickpeas, or torta del Casar, a soft sheep's cheese from the region that you eat with a spoon. Take water, and a hat, and allow an hour to walk along the dam and across the top, where you can see the water on one side and farmland on the other, the same view the Romans engineered.
t.fortlet of sao domingos@38.9,-7.2:
Elvas is a border town, and borders create walls. The town of Elvas, in the Alentejo, faces Spain across a short stretch of plain, with the Spanish fortress city of Badajoz only seventeen kilometres away, and for centuries the two countries glared at each other from behind stone. Portugal built what became the largest bulwarked dry-ditch fortification system in the world, and in 2012 the Garrison Border Town of Elvas and its Fortifications were inscribed on the World Heritage list. The little Fort of Sao Domingos is one of the smaller pieces in this puzzle, a fortlet set on the edge of the plain that strengthened the defence of the town.

The great set pieces are the star-shaped ramparts of Elvas itself, built in the seventeenth century under the influence of Dutch engineers, the Fort of Santa Luzia, and the Fort of Graca, a huge stronghold built on a hill in the 1760s. Most impressive of all is the Amoreira Aqueduct, a line of tall arches, some of them in four tiers, striding across the fields for over seven kilometres, which was begun in the sixteenth century and took more than a hundred years to finish. It still brings water to the town. In 1659 the Portuguese won the Battle of the Lines of Elvas here against a Spanish army, and that victory helped secure independence.

The riding in the Alentejo is relaxed. The land is wide and open, with cork oaks and olive groves scattered across gently rolling plains, golden in summer and green after the spring rains. The roads are long, smooth and often empty, with gentle curves and long views, and the main hazards are the heat, which can reach forty degrees in July and August, and the occasional storks that nest on lamp posts and church towers. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Early mornings in summer are sweet, but by mid afternoon the plain shimmers.

Elvas has nearly ten thousand people, so fuel and meals are no trouble. The town is famous for its sugar plums, which are preserved in syrup and eaten as dessert, and for its good bread and wine. Evora, with its Roman temple and bone chapel, is within an easy day's ride.
t.garrison border town of elvas and its fo:
Elvas sits ten kilometres from Spain, and it has the stonework to prove it. For centuries this small hilltop city in the Alentejo was Portugal's main defensive gate against its larger neighbour, the fortified town that faced Badajoz across the plain. The result is the largest system of bulwarked dry-ditch fortifications in the world, according to UNESCO, which listed it in 2012. The walls are in the star-shaped style that arrived in the seventeenth century, with sharp angled bastions, deep dry moats and protected paths, designed to withstand cannon. Two big forts stand on hills outside, a smaller one on another, and an aqueduct comes into town on gigantic arches.

The history is a record of wars between the two kingdoms. When Portugal broke away from Spain in 1640, Elvas became the front line for twenty-eight years of war, and in January 1659 a Spanish army besieged it. The Portuguese garrison, helped by the townspeople, sallied out and destroyed the Spanish lines, a victory remembered as the Battle of the Lines of Elvas. Later, in the Peninsular War, the Duke of Wellington used the town as a base.

You ride in through the walls, and the experience is half the pleasure: you pass under heavy gates, through narrow streets of whitewashed houses with wrought-iron balconies, to a central square paved with the black and white patterns of Portuguese calcada. Storks nest on chimneys and towers. Fuel and food are easy in this town of about ten thousand, and parking is best done outside the walls and followed by a walk.

The Alentejo is a country of cork oaks, olive groves, wheat fields and slow undulating plains that turn gold and parched by July, when temperatures routinely pass forty degrees. For riders, the main roads, including the A6 motorway and the older N4 from Lisbon, are smooth and fast, and the minor roads are quiet, with long views. Early spring brings wildflowers, and autumn brings mild days.

Elvas is famous for its plums, ameixas de Elvas, preserved in sugar syrup, and for sericaia, a baked pudding of egg and cinnamon served with plums. It would be rude to leave without trying both. Come in April, May or October for comfortable temperatures.
t.fortlet of sao mamede@38.9,-7.2:
A fortress the size of a small farm sits on a rise outside Elvas, and it is easy to ride past without noticing it. The Fortlet of Sao Mamede is one of the smaller pieces in the great defensive puzzle of this border town, an outpost on high ground whose job was to hold an approach and make life hard for anyone trying to besiege the main walls. It dates from the seventeenth century, the age of the Portuguese Restoration wars, when the country was fighting for independence from Spain and every hill on the border sprouted earthworks, a time when engineers sketched star-shaped plans from Dutch and Italian pattern books.

What makes these small works fascinating is how they fit together. Elvas was not defended by one wall but by a system: a main bastioned enceinte around the town, two big forts on hills outside, and a ring of smaller works placed to cover the gaps, all arranged so that their guns supported each other. A besieger who took one position found himself under fire from the next. It was a layered defence, planned like a game of chess, and the UNESCO listing in 2012 recognises the town and its forts as a single whole.

The fortlet is just outside the old town, about a kilometre away, in a landscape of olive trees, stone walls and fields. A rider can reach it by a short ride from the centre of Elvas along country lanes that are narrow, sometimes rough and often shared with a tractor or a flock of sheep. Elvas, about ten thousand people, has fuel, food and repairs, and the roads around it are mostly quiet.

Alentejo summers are fierce. Between June and September the sun hammers the plain and the heat shimmers off the tarmac, so ride early, carry water, and take lunch in the shade. Spring is the sweetest season, with wildflowers in the verges and storks feeding their young on the roofs, and autumn brings mild afternoons.

While you are here, find a cafe in the old town and ask for a slice of sericaia with plums, the baked egg pudding that Elvas has made its own.
t.amoreira aqueduct@38.9,-7.2:
Seven kilometres of arches carried water to Elvas, and the people of the town took a century to finish building them. The Amoreira Aqueduct was begun in the sixteenth century, when the old cisterns were no longer enough for a growing garrison town, and it was not finished until the early seventeenth, after a long stop and start, and a great deal of money, including a special tax on the townspeople. The result is a structure that strides across the plain on up to four tiers of arches, rising to about thirty metres, with hundreds of arches in all. It can be seen from far off, a long grey line over the fields, and where it comes into town it dwarfs the houses.

It was a defensive asset as well as a water supply. A besieged town without water falls quickly, so a fortress like Elvas needed an aqueduct inside the walls, and when you look at the final stretch, you can see the water channel running into a cistern in the heart of the city. It forms one of the elements of the UNESCO listing, which recognises the whole system as a unity of walls, forts and waterworks.

For a rider, the aqueduct is a pleasant detour. The roads into Elvas pass beneath it, and you can stop at a safe place, look up and photograph arches framed against the sky. It is tall and unusual enough to impress even after the forts. Fuel is easy in the town, and there are cafes in the square near the entrance.

The countryside is Alentejo at its most typical: low, rolling land with olive groves, cork oaks and stubble fields. In summer the grass turns the colour of lions, and in spring it is green and starred with flowers. Storks nest on the aqueduct itself in some years, building huge nests on top of the arches, and their clattering bills are a regular soundtrack.

Late afternoon is the best time to visit, when the low sun warms the stone and the shadows lengthen under the arches. Come in April or May, or in October, to avoid the heat of midsummer. The local plums are worth hunting for in the market.
t.fort of santa luzia and the covered way@:
From the top of the Fort of Santa Luzia you can look down on Elvas like a general planning an assault. The fort stands on a rise to the south of the old town and was built from 1641, at the start of the Portuguese Restoration War, to deny enemy artillery a hill that overlooked the walls. Its shape is a star, with four bastions and a deep dry ditch, and its engineers followed the Dutch style, which was the best defensive school in Europe at that time. The walls are thick and low, built to shed cannonballs, and the corridor called the covered way runs around the outer edge of the ditch, a protected path where soldiers could move in cover and meet an attack head on.

This was the position that the Spanish army attacked in January 1659, when they besieged Elvas, and it was the defenders' success in holding out that led to the victory in the Battle of the Lines of Elvas. The fort now houses a military museum, with cannon, uniforms, maps and swords, a fitting use for a place where so much of the story happened. It is one of the best-preserved examples of this kind of fort in Europe, which is why it forms part of the UNESCO site.

Walk along the covered way and the logic of the design becomes clear. You see how every wall is covered by another, how the ditch is overlooked from many angles, and how an attacker would have had no hiding place. It also gives you a good view of the aqueduct, the other forts and the plains of the Alentejo stretching toward Spain.

A short ride from the centre of Elvas, with parking at the gate, makes the visit easy. The roads are quiet and the fuel station and food are in town. Midsummer heat on exposed stone is fierce, so choose a morning visit or go in spring or autumn. The best light is in the late afternoon, when the walls turn gold.

Afterwards, find a restaurant in the old town and order a dish of migas, fried bread with pork, which is the classic Alentejo peasant dish, or a plate of the local ham.
t.historic centre@38.9,-7.2:
Climb through the gates of Elvas and the first thing you notice is how white everything is. Whitewashed houses with blue or yellow edging, wrought-iron balconies and doorways, climbing streets paved in small stones, with the occasional Moorish arch and the smell of coffee from a cafe. The old town sits on a hilltop inside its star-shaped walls, a place of narrow streets, small squares and churches, and its centre is much better kept than the usual garrison town. It was part of the UNESCO listing in 2012, and the old centre is the other half of the picture, the place that the fortifications protected.

The history goes back a long way. Elvas was a Moorish town before it was conquered by the Portuguese in the thirteenth century, and the castle at the top, with its Arabic origins and later additions, still dominates the skyline. The cathedral, once the main church, has a Renaissance character, and in the Largo de Santa Clara a stone pillory stands in front of a church. The octagonal Church of Nossa Senhora da Consolacao, with its domed interior covered in blue and white tiles, is the town's architectural treasure and well worth a few minutes.

Riding in is simple but you should leave the bike outside the walls, in one of the car parks near the gates, as the streets are narrow and cobbled. Fuel, banks and supermarkets are in the modern part of town, and you will find a good choice of restaurants and cafes inside the walls. The border with Spain is only a few kilometres away, and the N4 and the A6 motorway run straight to Lisbon, about two hundred kilometres to the west.

Alentejo food is hearty, with pork, lamb, bread soups and strong sheep cheese. Elvas is famed for its plums, which are preserved in sugar syrup, and the little pastry called sericaia. Wine from nearby estates is excellent value.

The plain around is hot in summer, with temperatures regularly passing forty degrees, so visit in spring or autumn. Early mornings are the best time to walk, before the streets fill with day-trippers from Spain. Look up as you walk: storks nest on towers and chimneys all over town.
t.fort of garca@38.9,-7.2:
The Fort of Graca sits on a hill north of Elvas, like a stone crown, and it was built after a lesson. In the 1750s and 1760s, Europe had been rocked by the Seven Years War, and Portugal, which had been dragged into conflict with Spain, found that its border defences were out of date. The government called in a foreign expert, the Count of Lippe, a German soldier of fortune and military reformer, who designed a new fortress on the highest hill overlooking the town. Work began in the 1760s and continued for decades, and the result was the most modern piece of the entire system, a fortress designed for the age of heavy artillery, with a star-shaped plan, deep ditches and underground galleries.

It is a big fort, with a large parade ground, a barracks, a chapel, powder stores and cisterns cut into the rock. The walls are lined with massive sloping banks to absorb cannon fire, and the tunnels let the garrison move without being seen. It was never put to the full test in a siege, but it has served in other ways, and in the twentieth century it also had a role as a prison. The UNESCO listing of 2012 includes it as one of the key elements of the Elvas system, a late example of the Dutch-style fortification that was the pride of the age.

From the walls you get the best view of the area: the old town below, the long line of the aqueduct crossing the plain, the other forts on their hills, and in the distance the Spanish plateau. On a clear day you can see for kilometres.

The road up is a short ride from the centre, a small winding lane with tight bends and a steep climb, so go carefully in the heat and watch for cyclists. Parking at the entrance is easy. Fuel and food are in Elvas, which is less than two kilometres away.

Check the opening times before you go, because access can vary, and guided visits may be needed. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with soft light and green countryside. In high summer the stone becomes an oven. A nice detail: wild thyme and rosemary grow on the slopes, and their scent rises in the evening.
t.evora@38.6,-7.9:
Alentejo is the part of Portugal that looks as if someone had ironed it. South and east of the Tagus, the land rolls out in low swells of wheat, olive and cork oak, with white villages on the hills and storks nesting on the chimneys, and Évora sits in the middle of it, about 130 kilometres east of Lisbon. It is a walled city of some fifty-five thousand, and for riders it is the natural pause in a long day of empty road.

The country around it is the montado, an open woodland of cork oaks and holm oaks with pasture beneath, where black Iberian pigs root for acorns and the cork is stripped from the trunks by hand every nine years or so, leaving the bare trunks a dull orange for a season. The roads that cross it are some of the most relaxed in western Europe: long, smooth straights, easy bends and wide skies, with few cars outside the towns. Distances are large and services thin, so fill the tank in Évora rather than gambling on the next village. Summer heat can reach forty degrees and more by mid-afternoon, and the hours between two and five are best spent under a roof; spring, when the fields are green and covered with poppies, and autumn, with the first rain and the cork harvest done, are far more comfortable.

A few kilometres west of the city, at Almendres, stand the biggest group of standing stones in the Iberian Peninsula, a cromlech of nearly a hundred granite monoliths set out on a hillside by Neolithic farmers around six thousand years ago. It is easy to reach down a track off the road and almost always quiet, with the stones casting long shadows at dawn and dusk. The nearby Anta Grande do Zambujeiro, a huge burial chamber, gives a similar sense of deep time.

Évora's food is simple and filling: migas, açorda, slow-cooked pork with clams, and sheep's cheese with wines from the surrounding estates. Dinner is late by northern standards, and many kitchens close in the afternoon.

Arrive in the early evening, when the heat softens, the stone of the old walls turns golden and the cafés fill.
t.historic centre of evora@38.6,-7.9:
Évora was Roman, Moorish, then Portuguese, and the centre of the city is a three-layered cake of all of them. The walled historic centre, a UNESCO site since 1986, is small enough to cross on foot in ten minutes, but it holds a Roman temple, a Gothic cathedral, a Renaissance aqueduct and a chapel decorated with human bones.

The temple, often called the Temple of Diana though nobody knows to whom it was dedicated, stands on a raised platform with its Corinthian columns still upright, built in the first century and preserved because it was used as a slaughterhouse and walled in for centuries. A few steps away, the cathedral's heavy granite towers recall a fortress, and from its roof you can see rooftops of white and orange stretching out to the plain. Then there is the Chapel of Bones, in the church of São Francisco, where Franciscan monks lined the walls with the skulls and bones of about five thousand people, with a warning above the door that reminds visitors of how little time they have.

Évora also had a university, founded in 1559 by the Jesuits and later closed by the Marquis of Pombal, which gave the city a scholarly air still visible in the cloisters and the students' cafés. t.ullapool@57.9,-5.2:

t.lisbon@38.7,-9.1:

t.seville@37.4,-6.0:

t.donana national park@36.9,-6.4:

t.south china karst@24.9,110.4:

t.glencoe@56.7,-5.1:

t.hong kong@22.3,114.2:

t.zone 2@22.2,113.6:

t.malin head@55.4,-7.4:

t.cabo da roca@38.8,-9.5:

t.serra@38.8,-8.8:

t.lisbon portugal@38.5,-8.6:

t.lagos@37.1,-8.7:

t.arrabida@38.9,-8.9:

t.casa herrera basilica@39.0,-6.3:

t.church of sta clara and visigothic art c:

It rises to about 626 metres, and it is closed in snow, and caravans and large vehicles are advised not to attempt it. Lochcarron is the sensible place to fill up and eat before you commit, since there is nothing at the top but a view and a very good wind.

The loch has seals and, in places, otters, and the castle ruins at Strome, a few kilometres on, stand on a point of land at the narrows. Midges can be fierce between June and August, particularly at dusk and on still days, and a repellent is more use than any amount of courage. Spring and early autumn are gentler, with clear air and fewer visitors on the road.

Kyle of Lochalsh and Plockton lie a little way south, with more services and the island of Skye just beyond.
t.tarbert@55.9,-5.4:
Tarbert is a fishing village on Loch Fyne, in Argyll, built around a harbor so snug that it looks like a painting. Its name comes from the Gaelic for a narrow neck of land across which boats could be dragged, a portage, and the old tale says that in 1098 the Norse king Magnus Barelegs had his longship hauled across this isthmus to claim the Kintyre peninsula as an island, and so a stretch of Scotland. A yacht race, the Scottish Series, fills the harbor each spring, and the whole village comes alive.

It runs south down the long Kintyre peninsula, past Skipness and Carradale, through hills and open moor, with views across to Arran and the Atlantic, and it forms the heart of the Kintyre 66 route. The road surface is variable, with some good fast sections and some patched ones, and curves are generally open, though a few tight bends catch the unwary. The weather is changeable, with rain and wind coming in off the sea, and the light on a clear day, with the islands floating on the horizon, is wonderful.

Campbeltown, further south, has more. The best months are May to September, though midges are a pest in still, humid weather. Winter storms can close the road, and ice is a risk. Keep an eye on the fuel gauge, because the peninsula is long and the stations are far between.
t.cushendun@55.1,-6.0:
Cushendun looks like a Cornish village that has been dropped, by mistake, on the coast of County Antrim, and in a sense it was. In the 1920s, the local landowner, Ronald McNeill, Lord Cushendun, commissioned the Welsh architect Clough Williams-Ellis, the creator of Portmeirion, to design a set of cottages around the green in memory of his Cornish wife. The result is a neat curve of whitewashed houses with slate roofs, now owned by the National Trust, and quite different in style from anything else on the Antrim coast. It is a quiet, small place, with a beach, a river mouth and a pub, and it has the feeling of a secret.

The village stands at the foot of Glendun, one of the nine Glens of Antrim, a series of deep green valleys cut into the plateau. Scotland is startlingly close here: on a clear day, the Mull of Kintyre can be seen across the North Channel, only about twenty kilometres away. The sea caves at the end of the beach, carved into red sandstone, have featured in a famous television fantasy series. Irish and Scottish Gaelic cultures have long mingled in this corner of the island, and the Glens still have a distinct identity.

The coast road between Cushendall and Ballycastle, the A2, is the best part of the Causeway route for riders. It rises and falls along the cliffs, with long sweeping views of the sea and the glens, bends that come in a pleasing rhythm, and a surface that is generally good. Traffic is lighter than on the Causeway end, though still busy in the summer holiday season. The weather can be changeable, with sea mist, drizzle and strong winds, and a clear day is a gift. The best time of year is late spring and early summer, when the gorse is in bloom and the days are long.

The scenery is gentle yet wild: green fields running to the cliff edge, white-washed farmhouses, and the dark outline of Rathlin Island on the horizon. Seabirds nest on the cliffs, and basking sharks and porpoises are sometimes spotted offshore in summer. Look for the carved wooden benches and small stone memorials along the route.

Cushendall, about eight kilometres to the south, has a petrol station, and Ballycastle, sixteen kilometres north-west, is the largest nearby town with supermarkets and services. A quiet stroll along the beach in the evening light is an excellent way to end the day.
t.carrick a rede@55.2,-6.3:
Fishermen first strung a rope bridge across the chasm at Carrick-a-Rede some two and a half centuries ago, so that they could reach a small island where Atlantic salmon swam close to the rocks on their way to the rivers. The view across the channel to Rathlin Island and the Scottish coast on a clear day is among the best on this coast. The crossing itself takes only a few minutes, and on the island, you can look back at the cliffs and watch seabirds wheeling below your feet, including fulmars, guillemots and razorbills. In windy weather the bridge closes, and there are timed tickets, which in summer should be booked online ahead of time, since walk-ups often find the day sold out.

The road to it, the B15, is a short, narrow coastal lane leaving the A2 near Ballintoy, with a few bends and gentle climbs, and the traffic in summer queues for the car park. It is a pleasant, rolling ride, with fields of sheep and cattle, low stone walls and sudden glimpses of the sea. Ballintoy Harbour, just along the coast, is a tiny cove with black basalt rocks, and it has appeared on screen as an island in a fantasy series. The lane down to it is steep and narrow, with a very tight turn at the bottom, so take it slowly.

Ballycastle, about seven kilometres to the east, has stations, shops and cafés, and it is also the ferry port for Rathlin Island. Arrive early or late to avoid the crowds, and take a warm layer, because the wind on the headland is cold.
t.giants causeway@55.2,-6.5:
About sixty million years ago, lava poured across what is now the Antrim coast, and as it cooled, it cracked into columns, most of them hexagonal, tens of thousands of them, packed together like a vast honeycomb. That, in short, is the Giant's Causeway, and the science is simple enough, though the sight is still strange. It was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

The legend is better. According to Irish tradition, the giant Finn McCool built the causeway as a path to Scotland so that he could fight his rival Benandonner, but when he saw how big the Scottish giant was, he ran home and disguised himself as a baby. Benandonner took one look at the size of the baby and fled in terror, tearing up the causeway behind him. Identical columns exist at Fingal's Cave on the Scottish island of Staffa, which gives the tale a certain geological logic.

In 1588, the Spanish Armada galleass Girona, carrying hundreds of survivors from other wrecked ships, was driven onto rocks near here, and nearly all aboard died. Portrush, about ten kilometres to the west, is the nearest sizeable town with fuel, supermarkets and seaside amusements. A bowl of seafood chowder with soda bread at a café in Bushmills is the standard lunch.
t.convent of christ in tomar@39.6,-8.4:
The Knights Templar chose the hill above Tomar in the twelfth century, building a castle to defend the new kingdom of Portugal against the Moors, and at its heart they raised a round church, the Charola, modelled on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. Over the centuries, the order added cloisters, chapels and dormitories, and the Convent of Christ became one of the great monuments of Portugal, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1983.

The Charola, its interior painted and gilded, is extraordinary, and so is the Manueline window on the west façade of the church, carved with ropes, coral, seaweed, armillary spheres and other symbols of the age of discovery. The great cloister, in Renaissance style, is calm and elegant. Allow a couple of hours to explore.

North, the mountains around Lousã and the schist villages offer twisting roads through forests and valleys. Tomar has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the local sweets, such as fatias de Tomar, and the regional dishes of roast meat and bacalhau. Spring and autumn are ideal, while summer can be very hot.
t.old town of caceres@39.5,-6.4:

Inside the walls, built largely by the Almohads in the twelfth century, are dozens of fortified mansions, towers, churches and palaces, many built by noble families who made their fortunes in the conquest of the Americas. The city is known for Torta del Casar, a creamy sheep's cheese from a nearby village, eaten by cutting off the top and scooping it out with bread, as well as Iberian ham and migas. Sit on the Plaza Mayor with a cold drink and watch the storks circle the towers.
t.monastery of batalha@39.7,-8.8:
On 14 August 1385, near the village of Aljubarrota, a Portuguese army led by King João I defeated a much larger Castilian force, securing Portugal's independence. Batalha is a small town of around eight thousand people, with fuel, shops and restaurants around the monastery square. The motorway passes close by, making it an easy stop on a journey between Lisbon and Porto. The weather is mild, with hot, dry summers and wet winters, and the limestone of the monastery glows golden in the evening sun.
t.cultural landscape of sintra@38.8,-9.4:
Lord Byron called Sintra a glorious Eden, and two centuries of romantics, kings and eccentric millionaires have tried hard to prove him right. On the peaks and in the woods stand the Moorish Castle, its walls snaking along the ridge; the Pena Palace, a riot of yellow and red towers built for King Ferdinand II in the mid-1800s; the Quinta da Regaleira, with its spiralling initiation well; and the exotic Monserrate palace. Its vines grow in deep sand near the ocean, which protected them from the phylloxera louse that destroyed most European vineyards in the nineteenth century, so many still grow on their own roots, sprawling low along the ground behind windbreaks. Just beyond, Cabo da Roca marks the westernmost point of mainland Europe, a windswept headland of cliffs and lighthouse where the Atlantic pounds the rocks far below.

The roads through the hills are narrow, twisting and often cobbled, slick when damp, with stone walls tight on both sides, and the town centre is a tangle of one-way streets choked with tuk-tuks, buses and tourists. In summer, traffic restrictions apply on the roads to the palaces. The rewards are the forest roads up to the Peninha sanctuary and over the ridge, and the coast road from Cascais via Guincho and Cabo da Roca, which is spectacular, windy and fast. Early mornings outside peak season are ideal.

In the old town, queue for travesseiros, puff-pastry pillows filled with almond cream, and queijadas, small cheese tarts, both famous local sweets. The palaces each take time, so choose one or two rather than trying to see everything in a day, and pack a layer: Sintra is often cool and foggy when Lisbon is basking in sunshine.
t.medina of tetouan@35.6,-5.4:
Tétouan wears its Andalusian heritage in whitewash. Spanish is still widely understood, and the cafes of the Plaza Hassan II, the old Plaza de España, are favourite spots for a long mint tea. Tétouan is a city of over three hundred thousand, so fuel is plentiful, and the road to the coast at Martil is short. The route from Chefchaouen, on the ride list, is the great reward. It threads through the Rif on bends and ridges, with cork oaks, pines and village houses in blue and white, and the surface varies from good to broken. Heavy rain and fog can come down in the mountains in winter and spring.

Spring is the best season, with green slopes and cool mornings, and autumn is also good. Summers on the coast are hot and busy with Moroccans on holiday, so book ahead.

Eat in the medina if you can. A plate of grilled sardines, a bowl of harira soup and a pastry from one of the almond sweet shops will set the day right.
t.monastery of the hieronymites and tower:
In Belém, the river Tagus widens toward the Atlantic, and the whole district has the feel of a farewell. This was where Portuguese ships left for India, Brazil and the spice islands, and where the returning ones anchored, laden with pepper, cinnamon and gold. A good deal of that wealth went into building. The Mosteiro dos Jerónimos, begun in 1501 under King Manuel I and paid for in part by a levy on the spice trade, and the Tower of Belém, finished in 1519, are the twin pillars of a style that takes its name from the king, Manueline, with carved ropes, anchors, armillary spheres and exotic plants in stone. Together they were listed by UNESCO in 1983.

The riverside is the place to get a sense of it. A long promenade runs from the tower past the Padrão dos Descobrimentos, a monument shaped like the prow of a caravel with Prince Henry the Navigator in front, opened in 1960, and along the shore towards the great red suspension bridge, the Ponte 25 de Abril, which resembles the Golden Gate. Behind them, in the pastry shop on Rua de Belém, the custard tarts have been baked to a secret recipe since 1837, and the queue at the door is a part of the experience.

Lisbon is a good place for a bike and a bad place to park one. The streets climb in steep, cobbled lanes, and the old trams, rails and wet stone are treacherous in the rain. In Belém, the roads are wide and flat and easy, with free or cheap places for motorcycles near the river, but check the signs because the police do ticket. The riding is all about leaving town. The coast road west towards Cascais, past Estoril and the Atlantic beaches, is a joy, and then the road to Sintra, which climbs into misty hills with palaces and forest, is part of the same ride list.

Fuel is easy in a metropolis of this size, and stations along the Marginal, the main coast road, are frequent. In summer the Atlantic fog can roll in over Cascais in the afternoon, so the temperature drops sharply.

Come early in the day, before the coach tours arrive, and finish with a coffee and a pastel de nata on the benches near the river.
t.tower of belem@38.7,-9.2:
The Tower of Belém was never really a defensive tower, though it looks like a stronghold. King Manuel I ordered it built in 1514 on a rocky islet near the north bank of the Tagus, as part of a system of fortifications guarding the river mouth and the route to Lisbon, with cannon on the lower platform and living quarters above. Francisco de Arruda, who had worked in Morocco, designed it, and the style mixes Gothic, Moorish and Renaissance touches with the Manueline repertoire of ropes, shields with the Cross of the Order of Christ, and stone sails. A tiny stone rhinoceros under one of the turrets is often described as the first European sculpture of the animal, a creature that had arrived in Lisbon in 1515 as a gift for the Pope, and which Dürer famously drew from a description.

The Tagus has changed its course since then. Over the centuries the riverbank has shifted and silt has built up, so the tower, which once stood in the water, is now joined to the shore by a short walkway. The earthquake of 1755, which devastated much of Lisbon, damaged it but spared much of the stonework, and it was a prison for a time, then restored in the nineteenth century. UNESCO listed it with the Jerónimos Monastery in 1983.

To go inside means to climb narrow spiral staircases, and queues can be long in summer, so go early. The terrace on top offers a view over the river, with ships heading out beneath the great bridge. It is a good place to watch the light on the water, and especially lovely in the late afternoon, when the stone turns golden.

On a motorcycle, the riverside is simple, with a wide road, plenty of parking and views of the water, though wind off the Atlantic can be strong. The ride list heads north to Mafra, where a monumental baroque palace and monastery built with Brazilian gold fills a vast front of white stone, an hour's ride through Lisbon's outskirts and then the rolling farmland of the Estremadura. Fuel is plentiful on the way, and Algés, a short distance upriver, has stations on the main road.

Try the grilled sardines of summer in a nearby tasca, and keep your helmet for the bike.
t.monastery of the hieronymites@38.7,-9.2:
The Hieronymites were a monastic order that followed Saint Jerome, and King Manuel I gave them a very grand home. He ordered the monastery built on the riverbank at Belém in 1501, on the site of a small chapel founded by Henry the Navigator, to serve as a royal pantheon and a place where monks would pray for sailors and for the king's soul, and it took most of a century to complete. The church inside is calm after the exuberance of the portal, with tall, slender pillars like palm trees holding a star-patterned vault. The tombs include that of Vasco da Gama, who opened the sea route to India in 1498, and of the poet Luís de Camões, who wrote the epic about that voyage, The Lusiads. The modern poet Fernando Pessoa is also buried here, moved in 1985 to this national shrine. The monks stayed until 1834, when religious orders were abolished in Portugal, after which the building served as an orphanage and school.

The road from Lisbon to Tomar runs about an hour and a half north through the Ribatejo, a country of olive groves, vineyards and wide fields along the Tagus, with plenty of quiet roads.

In Belém the street plan is easy, though it can be busy at weekends. Bikes can usually be parked in the car parks near the monastery and along the river, and the district has fuel and cafes. The queue for the monastery church and cloister can be long, but it moves.

Go in the late afternoon if you can, when the light comes through the cloister arcades and the crowd thins, and take a moment to look at the stone vines and ropes on the capitals, each one slightly different.
t.fortlet of sao pedro@38.9,-7.2:

The Amoreira Aqueduct, with its tall arches, runs into Elvas from the countryside, built over a hundred years from the late fifteenth century, and it is a fine sight at sunset.

The surface is smooth, the bends are gentle, and traffic is light, with storks nesting on poles and church towers, and flocks of sheep under the cork trees. In summer, the heat is formidable, with temperatures above forty degrees, and the plain shimmers, so start before dawn and finish early. Spring brings green fields and wildflowers, the best moment, and autumn has soft light and the cork harvest has just finished. The border with Spain is open and unmarked, so you may cross without noticing, apart from the clock, because Spain is an hour ahead of Portugal.

Elvas has fuel and supermarkets, and is famous for its sugared plums, Ameixas d'Elvas, and for a rich pork stew with the local olive oil. A town of ten thousand has plenty of places to eat, and Badajoz, across the border, is a city of nearly 150,000 with a big range of shops. The ride list continues to Alange, a small spa town in Extremadura where the Romans built thermal baths that are still in use.

A cold drink in the main square, under the arches, is the best way to end a hot day.
t.the mithraeum house the columbaria funer:
Mérida was founded in 25 BC as Emerita Augusta, a colony for veterans of Augustus's Cantabrian wars, and for centuries it was one of the greatest cities of Roman Spain, capital of the province of Lusitania. It still has a theatre and an amphitheatre side by side, a circus that could hold tens of thousands, a bridge over the Guadiana of about 790 metres that remains in use, and an aqueduct whose brick-and-granite piers rise above the road like the legs of a giant. Mithras was a god of soldiers and merchants, worshipped in underground chambers, and Mérida, full of veterans, would have been a natural home for the cult. Next door the Columbaria are tombs, with niches in the walls where the ashes of the dead were placed, and their painted decoration is a reminder that Romans buried their dead close to the road and in company.

Mérida is simple to reach and easy to like. From Cáceres or Badajoz the road crosses dehesa, oak parkland dotted with black Iberian pigs and cork trees, and the riding is fast and open with broad bends and little traffic. In summer the temperature in Extremadura can soar above forty degrees, so plan to be here in spring or autumn, and never leave a jacket on the saddle in July. Calamonte, five kilometres away, and the other satellite towns offer plenty of fuel.

Eating here means jamón, the soft cheese called torta del Casar, and wines of the Ribera del Guadiana, and the old centre has plenty of terraces on the shaded squares. The Roman monuments are best seen early or late, when the stone is warm and there are fewer visitors. Some twenty kilometres to the south-east, the thermal baths at Alange have been used since Roman times and make a good restful side trip after a hot day in the saddle. Leave the bike in a paying car park rather than on a street near the monuments.
t.ronda@36.7,-5.2:
Ronda is built on both sides of a gorge, and nobody quite believes it until they stand on the bridge. The Tajo, a cleft some hundred metres deep, cuts the town in two, and the Guadalevín river runs along its bottom. The Puente Nuevo, a tall stone bridge finished in the late eighteenth century after earlier collapses, joins the old Moorish quarter to the newer town on the other side, and the views from the viewpoints around it, down the cliff and out over the plain, are among the best in Andalusia.

The town has a long past. The Romans and then the Moors settled the rocky platform, and Ronda was a stronghold of the Muslim rulers until it fell to the Catholic monarchs in 1485. t.gaucin@36.5,-5.3:

t.zahara@36.8,-5.4:

t.obidos@39.4,-9.2:

t.sesimbra@38.4,-9.1:

t.estremoz@38.8,-7.6:

t.sines@38.0,-8.9:

t.aljezur@37.3,-8.8:

t.monchique@37.3,-8.6:

t.silves@37.2,-8.4:

Setúbal is a working port city at the mouth of the Sado estuary, the sort of place that tourists tend to skip and locals quietly love. Fishing boats, ferries and cargo ships share the water, and across the estuary the long, flat sand spit of Tróia stretches out. The city is proud of its food. Choco frito, fried cuttlefish strips, is the local dish, and grilled fish is usually fresh and simply cooked. In Colares, the vines grow in sand. The vineyards, on the dunes near the Atlantic, are dug deep into the sand to reach the clay beneath, and the vines, low and sprawling, are protected from the wind by fences of cane. Because phylloxera, the insect that destroyed Europe's vineyards in the nineteenth century, cannot survive in sand, the Ramisco vines of Colares were never grafted, and some are very old. The wine is rare, tannic and long-lived, a curiosity of Portuguese wine.

Colares is a village at the foot of the Sintra hills, between the mountains and the sea. Sintra, a few kilometres east, is famous for its palaces, the colourful Pena Palace on the summit, the Moorish Castle on the ridge and the mysterious Quinta da Regaleira, with its initiation well. The hills are often wrapped in mist, even in summer, giving them a romantic, otherworldly feel.

West of Colares, the village of Azenhas do Mar clings to a cliff above the sea, its white houses stacked above an ocean pool. Cabo da Roca, a little south, is the westernmost point of continental Europe, a windswept headland with a lighthouse and a monument.

The riding is superb but demanding. The roads through the Sintra hills are narrow, steep and winding, often cobbled and damp, with tourist traffic and buses. The coast road is more open, with views over the sea. Watch for fog, wet cobbles and wind.

Fill up in Sintra or on the main roads before diving into the hills. Then take lunch near the sea, at Azenhas do Mar or Praia das Maçãs, where an old tram still clatters down from Sintra in summer; grilled fish and a glass of sandy-soil Colares red make a lunch you will remember long after the cobbles have stopped rattling in your wrists.
